title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
writer: Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens & Peter Jackson
cast: Elijah Wood, Ian McKellen, Viggo Mortensen & Sean Astin
basis: J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Fellowship of the Ring, with material rearranged from the wider story
overview: A small traveler accepts a dangerous burden as companions confront fear, temptation, and divided loyalties. Study quest structure, characterization, and the limits of individual power.
essential: What makes a person trustworthy when power offers an easier path?
goals: Explain how power & temptation shapes character choices.
Support an interpretation with two accurately described scenes.
Compare the portrayal with a selected passage from its source or another relevant text.
prep: Use the approximately 178-minute theatrical edition; the extended edition is about 208 minutes and adds scenes. Introduce quest, motif, exposition, and temptation. This is the first film in a larger story, so its ending intentionally leaves the main quest unfinished.
context: Compare a teacher-selected Tolkien passage with its film scene. The adaptation omits episodes such as Tom Bombadil and moves some events across book boundaries; Boromir’s death appears in the next book. Discuss fantasy symbols as interpretations rather than forcing a single allegory.
pauses: Pause after the departure from the Shire, after the Council of Elrond, after Moria, and when the Fellowship separates.
warnings: Frequent fantasy combat, arrows, stabbing, decapitation or injury detail, and deaths.
Frightening monsters, pursuit, dark environments, and intense peril.
Smoking and drinking; disturbing transformation and temptation scenes.
discussion: What makes a person trustworthy when power offers an easier path?
Which scene best supports your interpretation, and what might another viewer notice?
What does the film leave out or simplify?

online.question: Why might power tempt someone who intends to do good?
online.answer: It can promise quick solutions while changing how that person treats others.

online.question: What makes a quest different from a simple journey?
online.answer: A difficult purpose, obstacles, and changing responsibilities shape the traveler.

online.question: Why does Gandalf investigate Bilbo’s ring?
online.answer: He suspects that it is the dangerous One Ring rather than an ordinary possession.

online.question: Why must Frodo leave the Shire?
online.answer: Remaining there would expose him and the community to those seeking the Ring.

online.question: How does Sam’s decision to accompany Frodo establish loyalty?
online.answer: He accepts risk and supports a friend beyond familiar surroundings.

online.question: What makes the Black Riders threatening?
online.answer: They pursue the Ring and create danger even when the hobbits try to hide.

online.question: How does Aragorn help the travelers before Rivendell?
online.answer: He guides and protects them while they learn to judge his character.

online.section: Part B · Forming and testing the Fellowship
online.question: What does Frodo’s injury reveal about the quest’s danger?
online.answer: The threat can harm him directly and requires help beyond his own abilities.

online.section: Part B · Forming and testing the Fellowship
online.question: Why can the Ring not simply be kept or used safely by the group?
online.answer: Its corrupting power makes possession and intended use dangerous.

online.section: Part B · Forming and testing the Fellowship
online.question: Why does Frodo volunteer at the council?
online.answer: He accepts responsibility when others disagree about how to carry the burden.

online.section: Part B · Forming and testing the Fellowship
online.question: What does the Fellowship’s mixed membership make possible?
online.answer: Different skills and perspectives support a task no member can complete alone.

online.section: Part B · Forming and testing the Fellowship
online.question: Why do the companions enter Moria?
online.answer: Their route options narrow, leading them to a dangerous passage through the mountains.

online.question: How does Gandalf’s fall affect the group?
online.answer: They lose a guide and must continue through grief and uncertainty.

online.question: How does Galadriel’s response illustrate temptation?
online.answer: She recognizes the promise of power and ultimately refuses to take the Ring.

online.question: Why does Boromir try to take the Ring?
online.answer: He believes it could help his people, but desire for its power overwhelms his restraint.

online.question: Why does Frodo leave, and why does Sam follow?
online.answer: Frodo fears further corruption of companions; Sam refuses to let him carry the burden alone.

online.question: Choose a moment when restraint shows strength.
online.answer: Accept refusal of the Ring or another supported example of resisting an easy use of power.

online.question: How does the film make a small protagonist seem important?
online.answer: Accept contrasts of scale, framing, attention to choices, or companions’ responses.

online.question: Why is the ending not a complete resolution of the larger conflict?
online.answer: The quest continues after the Fellowship separates; this film is one part of the story.

online.question: What effect might removing a novel episode have on the adaptation?
online.answer: It can change pace, world-building, or themes; explain with a teacher-selected comparison.
